title: Teaching Machines to Hear Better Than People
summary:
The crack of a bat and the cheers of a crowd can tell a baseball fan that something exciting happened, even without seeing it. At MIT, Professor Paris Smaragdis wants machines that hear and understand sounds even better than people.

It could hear a traffic accident in squealing tires and crunching metal, or tell when a drill digging a geothermal well might break. He says his work does for hearing what computer vision does for seeing.

Smaragdis joined MIT in 2025 and leads a group studying machine learning, sound source separation, and music tools.

Music started his journey. He grew up in Greece, played classical guitar, and later used computers and synthesizers at Berklee College of Music in Boston, where he majored in bass.

With mentor Richard Boulanger, he made music tools. Then he worked with Professor Barry Vercoe at the MIT Media Lab.

He then turned to teaching computers to understand sound, choosing machine learning. He believes we must teach computers how to listen, because we cannot simply tell them how.
why_it_matters: If machines learn to listen well, they could one day warn people about dangers like crashes before anyone even sees them.

keywords.explanation: Geothermal means heat that comes from deep inside the Earth and can be used for energy.
Synthesizers are electronic instruments that can make many different sounds.
Machine learning is a way for computers to learn from examples instead of being told every single step.
Computer vision is how computers learn to understand pictures and video.
Sound source separation means picking out one sound from a mix of many sounds happening at once.

background_read: Machine learning is a way of teaching computers by showing them lots of examples, so they can learn to spot patterns on their own instead of following simple step-by-step orders.
Computer vision does the same kind of job for seeing, helping computers make sense of pictures and video.
Paris Smaragdis wants to bring that idea to hearing, so machines can pick out important sounds, like a crash or a breaking drill, and understand what they mean.
Article_Structure: WHO: Paris Smaragdis, who leads a group at MIT studying machine learning, sound, and music tools.
WHAT: He is working on machines that hear and understand sounds even better than people.
WHERE: At MIT, after earlier work at Berklee College of Music in Boston and the MIT Media Lab.
WHY: So machines can notice important sounds, like a traffic accident or a drill about to break, and understand what they mean.
